messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Adebayo had spent forty years as a man in complete control of his environment. As a senior bomb disposal technician, his life was a study in precision, calm, and the meticulous management of threat. That control evaporated eight months ago during a routine call to a decommissioned industrial site. The device wasn't explosive but chemical, a corroded canister of nerve agent rigged to a pressure-plate trigger. As he began the delicate work of neutralizing it, the canister’s casing failed with a percussive, deafening crack. A colourless, acrid gas filled the small concrete room. His last memory before his respirator-clad colleagues dragged him out was of a searing pain in his lungs and the overwhelming, sterile smell of the decontamination tent, a smell that would later merge in his mind with the antiseptic corridors of the military hospital where he spent the next two weeks.

Since returning to his post, the very workplace that once defined his competence has become a landscape of invisible threats. The familiar clang of a dropped tool or the sudden hiss of a pneumatic line can send a jolt of pure terror through him, leaving him breathless and scanning the room for an enemy he cannot see. This constant, exhausting state of high alert is now his baseline. At his workstation, his eyes are never still, constantly tracking the movement of others, mapping the quickest path to the exits. He has come to believe that danger is not an event, but the very air he breathes, and that only his vigilance keeps him alive. This heightened sense of threat has, in turn, made him exquisitely sensitive to the triggers themselves; he finds himself flinching at the sound of a truck backfiring a block away, his body already reacting as if the concrete room were collapsing around him again.

The triggers at work and the pervasive sense of danger they ignite have driven Adebayo into a new, rigid set of routines. He has started working punishingly long hours, volunteering for every extra shift, not out of duty, but to avoid the silence of being alone with his thoughts. The antiseptic smell of the base's cleaning supplies, so similar to the hospital, sends a wave of nausea through him, and in response, he has begun to rigorously avoid the on-base medical clinic, twice faking an off-site emergency to miss his mandatory annual physical. He knows, on some level, that this is unsustainable, but the thought of a doctor's office, with its sterile scents and probing questions, feels more dangerous than any unexploded ordnance.

These strategies, meant to provide safety, have only tightened the cage. The excessive hours he works to escape his own mind mean that when he finally returns home, the quiet house he shares with his wife, Funke, feels cavernous and menacing. Being alone in a room, once a source of peace, now feels like an invitation for ambush. He finds himself pacing the halls at night, checking locks, and planning how he would get Funke out if the house were ever compromised. His avoidance has not diminished the threat; it has expanded its territory until even his own home feels like hostile ground. When Funke, worried by the dark circles under his eyes, gently touches his arm to get his attention, he recoils with an alarming shout, his body reacting to her loving gesture as if it were a mortal blow.

It was after one such incident last week, seeing the deep hurt and fear in his wife’s eyes as he backed away from her touch, that Adebayo finally made this appointment. The man who could calmly defuse a bomb with seconds to spare now feels like a stranger in his own body, a prisoner to a nervous system that screams danger at every turn. He came to therapy not with a clear hope, but with a desperate fear: that the control he has lost is gone for good, and that he is becoming a danger to the one person he has always felt safe with.
